annotations.title: Get every planet's position on a date

description:
Returns where every body is at an instant, with no birth data and no place required: Sun, Moon, the eight planets and the two lunar nodes, each with geocentric ecliptic longitude, sign and degree in both the tropical (Western) and sidereal (Vedic) zodiacs, ecliptic latitude, longitude speed in degrees per day, retrograde state and distance. It covers "what sign is Venus in", "where is Mercury right now", "what sign is the Moon in today", "when did Mars enter Gemini": any position question about the sky with no particular person's chart in it.

A geocentric longitude is identical for every observer on Earth, so a sky question needs no birthplace and no chart. An observer's lat and lon are used only for rise and set times.

A planet sits within a degree of a cusp for days, so "Venus is in Scorpio" can be true on Tuesday and false on Wednesday; the Moon moves about half a degree an hour and changes sign roughly every 2.3 days, so its row depends on the hour as well as the date. "time" is UTC and defaults to 00:00.

Both zodiacs come back in every row: result.bodies[].sign is the tropical sign and result.bodies[].siderealSign the sidereal one. They differ by result.ayanamsa, about 24 degrees, very nearly a whole sign, so the two are usually different signs. Rahu and Ketu are the mean nodes (result.nodeNote). result.retrogradeNow lists which of the eight stationing bodies are retrograde; the two nodes, which move backwards every day, are reported apart in result.alwaysRetrograde.

Results include an attribution line and a permalink.

date.description: The date, ISO YYYY-MM-DD, 1700-2200. Example: "2026-09-21". Defaults to today (UTC).

lat.description: Observer latitude in decimal degrees as a string. Example: "64.1466". Paired with lon. Rise and set only.

lon.description: Observer longitude in decimal degrees as a string. Example: "-21.9426". Paired with lat. Rise and set only.

place.description: Observer town or city. Example: "Reykjavik, Iceland". Optional; it changes no position, only rise and set times.

time.description: Time of day HH:MM, read as UTC. Example: "12:00". Matters for the Moon, which moves about half a degree an hour.

tz.description: IANA zone or numeric UTC offset hours for the local rise and set times. Example: "Atlantic/Reykjavik".

name: get_planetary_positions
title: Get every planet's position on a date
